title: Editing generated text
description: The tells readers now recognise, the cutting pass that improves almost any draft, putting back the specifics only you have, and the two-minute read-aloud that catches everything else.

modules.title: The course
modules.description: Four lessons on the skill that decides whether text reads as yours.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Readers can now spot generated text, and they are increasingly annoyed by it. Not because it is bad — because it signals that nobody spent any attention on them.

The tells are consistent and short in number, which means they can be removed systematically rather than by instinct.

blocks.heading: Eight words and phrases
blocks.bodyHtml:
• «delve», «leverage», «robust», «seamless»
  • «It's not just X, it's Y» — the most recognisable structure of all
  • «In today's fast-paced world»
  • «Let's dive in» and «Here's the thing»
  • Three adjectives where one would do

A single find-and-replace pass on this list changes how a piece reads more than an hour of rewriting.

blocks.text: Readers are not annoyed that it was generated. They are annoyed that nobody looked at it.

blocks.heading: The structural tells matter more
blocks.bodyHtml:
Words are easy. The shape is what gives it away.

Three tidy points of equal length, then a paragraph summarising the three points.

Two points of different weight, one of them with an example, and no summary because you already made it.

Human writing is uneven. Perfectly balanced structure is the strongest tell there is.

blocks.question: Which is the strongest signal to a reader that text was generated?

options.label: Occasional spelling mistakes and small inconsistencies in the wording.
Perfectly balanced structure with a closing paragraph that summarises.
A long piece of writing covering the subject in considerable detail.
Formal vocabulary and complete sentences throughout the whole piece.

blocks.successBody: Even weighting and a tidy recap are the clearest structural tell, because people do not naturally write that way. Mistakes read as human, and length or formality are choices anyone might make.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what human writing looks like when nobody has tidied it — is it evenly balanced?

blocks.heading: Fix the shape first
blocks.bodyHtml:
Removing banned words from a perfectly symmetrical piece leaves a perfectly symmetrical piece with different words.

Break the balance: delete the weakest point entirely, expand one, cut the summary. That single edit does more than every word substitution combined.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a generated draft and find the eight tells in it.
Delete the closing summary paragraph and see whether anything is lost.
Remove the weakest of the three points entirely.
Expand one remaining point with a real example.

blocks.title: Match the tell to how strong it is
blocks.subtitle: Match each feature of a draft with how clearly it signals its origin.

left.text: Three points of identical weight and a recap

right.text: The strongest structural tell there is

left.text: An occasional typo or uneven sentence

right.text: Reads as human rather than machine

left.text: One real number from your own experience

right.text: Makes the whole piece read as yours

blocks.failHint: Think about what unedited human writing actually looks like — is it evenly balanced?

blocks.heading: Keep one thing only you could write
blocks.bodyHtml:
The most reliable fix is to add something that could not have been generated: a real number, a specific mistake you made, the name of an actual client, what happened last Tuesday.

One such sentence makes an entire piece read as human, even if everything around it was drafted by a tool.

blocks.body: The tells are a short list of words and, more importantly, a perfectly even structure with a summarising ending. Fix the shape before the vocabulary — delete the weakest point, expand another, cut the recap — and add at least one thing only you could have written.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated text is almost always too long. Not padded exactly — every sentence is doing something — but doing it at a leisurely pace nobody asked for.

Cutting is the highest-value edit available and the one people are most reluctant to do, because deleting feels like waste.

blocks.heading: Cut a third and see
blocks.bodyHtml:
The reliable experiment: remove a third of the words without removing any information, then compare.

«It's important to note that there are several factors which may contribute to this outcome.»

«Three things cause this.»

Fourteen words to four, and the second is clearer. That ratio is typical, not exceptional.

blocks.text: If cutting a third loses nothing, the third was never doing anything.

blocks.heading: What to delete first
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The opening paragraph — it is almost always a warm-up
  • «It's important to note that» and every phrase like it
  • The closing summary — you already said it
  • The second and third adjective
  • Any sentence starting «Additionally» or «Moreover»

Delete all five and read what remains. It is usually the piece you wanted.

blocks.question: You cut a generated draft by a third and it reads better. What does that tell you?

options.label: The draft was unusually poor and should have been regenerated instead.
Generated text runs long by default, so cutting should be routine.
The original prompt was too vague and needs to be much more specific.
You removed necessary detail and the piece is now incomplete.

blocks.successBody: Length is the default, not a fault of that particular draft, which is why cutting belongs in the process every time rather than being treated as a fix for a bad result.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask whether this was a one-off problem or something you should expect every time.

blocks.heading: Ask for the short version
blocks.bodyHtml:
You can do half of this by asking: «same information, half the length, keep the example».

Then cut the short version by hand as well. Two passes, and the second one is where the piece actually becomes yours.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take any draft and delete the first paragraph.
Remove every sentence beginning with a transition word.
Ask for it at half the length and compare with your own cut.
Count the words you ended up with against where you started.

blocks.heading: Length is not value
blocks.bodyHtml:
Longer output feels like more work and more value. Readers experience it as more time spent, which is the opposite.

The piece someone finishes is worth more than the thorough one they abandon halfway — and shorter is almost always the version they finish.

blocks.body: Generated text is long by default, so cutting belongs in the process every time. Delete the opening paragraph, the transition sentences, the closing summary and the extra adjectives, ask for a half-length version, then cut that by hand too.
blocks.nextTeaser: Next: putting the specifics back in.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Cutting removes what should not be there. It does not add what is missing — and what is missing is almost always the same thing.

Generated text drifts towards the general, because the general is the safest average of everything. Specifics are what you have to supply.

blocks.heading: Replace categories with instances
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Many businesses struggle to keep their content consistent.»

«A bakery I worked with posted daily for three weeks, then stopped for two months.»

The second is the same point made concrete. It is also unarguable, because it happened.

blocks.text: Nobody remembers a category. Everybody remembers an instance.

blocks.heading: Four kinds worth adding
blocks.bodyHtml:
• A number — «three weeks», not «a while»
  • A named thing — a tool, a place, a real example
  • A quote — what someone actually said
  • A failure — what did not work, and why

The fourth is the most persuasive and the least used. Nobody generates admissions of failure, so they read as unmistakably real.

blocks.question: A generated paragraph is accurate but forgettable. What is most likely missing?

options.label: Stronger vocabulary to make the writing more vivid and memorable.
A specific instance — a number, a name or something that happened.
A clearer structure so the argument is easier for readers to follow.
A stated conclusion, so the reader knows what to take away from it.

blocks.successBody: Forgettable almost always means general. One number or one real example makes a paragraph stick, while stronger words make a general statement sound more emphatic without becoming more memorable.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what you remember from things you read last week — the phrasing, or the details?

blocks.heading: Only you have this material
blocks.bodyHtml:
This is the part of writing no tool can do, and therefore the part worth your time. Your numbers, your clients, your mistakes.

Keep a running note of them — the odd figure, the thing that went wrong, the exact phrase a customer used. That file is what turns a competent draft into something worth reading.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take a generated paragraph and find every general statement in it.
Replace one with something specific from your own experience.
Add one number, even an approximate one you can stand behind.
Start a note file for specifics as you come across them.

blocks.heading: One per paragraph is enough
blocks.bodyHtml:
You do not need to rewrite everything. One concrete detail per paragraph transforms a piece, and it is achievable in ten minutes.

Chasing more than that produces a different failure — a piece so dense with examples that the argument disappears underneath them.

blocks.body: Generated text drifts general, so add what it cannot know: a number, a named thing, a real quote, a failure. One specific per paragraph is enough to transform a piece, and keeping a running note of your own material is what makes that fast.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
The last pass takes two minutes, requires no skill, and catches more than every other technique in this course combined.

Read the whole thing out loud. Everything wrong with it becomes audible in a way it never is on screen.

blocks.heading: What your ear catches
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Sentences you run out of breath in — too long
  • Words you would never say — «utilise», «myriad», «furthermore»
  • The place you stumble — a real ambiguity, every time
  • Repetition — invisible on screen, obvious aloud
  • Flat rhythm — every sentence the same length

None of these are visible while reading silently, because your eye smooths over what your mouth cannot.

blocks.text: Where you stumble reading aloud, a reader stumbles silently and blames you for it.

blocks.heading: Vary the length on purpose
blocks.bodyHtml:
Every sentence between fifteen and twenty words, evenly, for three paragraphs.

A long sentence that builds through several clauses and takes its time. Then a short one. That contrast is what rhythm is.

Generated text is metrically even, and even rhythm reads as machine-made even when every individual sentence is fine.

blocks.question: Reading aloud, you stumble over the same sentence twice. What does that mean?

options.label: You are reading too quickly and should slow down for that section.
The sentence is genuinely ambiguous and needs rewriting, not rereading.
The vocabulary is too advanced and should be simplified for readers.
The sentence is too long and should simply be split into two parts.

blocks.successBody: A stumble is your own comprehension failing in real time, and a silent reader hits the same problem without noticing why. Splitting it may be the fix, but the diagnosis is ambiguity rather than length.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask what your stumble is telling you about how the sentence will be read by someone else.

blocks.heading: Read the first line twice
blocks.bodyHtml:
If nothing else, read the opening aloud. It is the sentence most people never revisit and the one that decides whether the rest is read at all.

Generated openings are reliably the weakest part of a piece, because they were produced before the argument existed.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take something you are about to send and read it aloud fully.
Mark every place you stumble or run out of breath.
Rewrite only those sentences and nothing else.
Read it again and see how many remain.

blocks.heading: The whole process, in order
blocks.bodyHtml:
Cut a third. Fix the structure. Add one specific per paragraph. Read aloud. Ship.

Ten minutes on a normal piece. That routine is the entire difference between text that reads as yours and text everyone recognises — and none of it requires being a good writer.

blocks.body: Reading aloud catches long sentences, unnatural words, real ambiguity, repetition and flat rhythm — none of which are visible on screen. Vary sentence length deliberately, always read the opening, and run the full routine: cut, restructure, add specifics, read aloud.
